name: Orchard District
label: Orchard District
about_prose: Orchard District sits in central-northeast Bend, in the area residents and the city call Midtown. The neighborhood association's own map draws the boundary from Pilot Butte on the east to the BNSF railroad and the US-97 Parkway on the west, with Franklin Avenue as the south edge and Butler Market Road as the north. That puts most of the neighborhood about a mile from downtown, close enough that the NE 6th Street Neighborhood Greenway, one of Bend's first, carries cyclists and walkers the length of the district from Greenwood Avenue to Butler Market Road on calmed streets with speed humps and marked crossings instead of a painted bike lane on a busy arterial.

The name comes from a real, failed business rather than a marketing flourish. In the 1930s, growers planted a commercial apple orchard on the land now behind Wagner Mall, betting that the area's slightly lower elevation and its shelter from Bend's prevailing wind would keep frost off the trees through more of the season. The commercial orchard did not survive, but the warmer pocket of air it was built on did, and longtime residents still call it the banana belt. A handful of buildings from that era, including the orchard's original farmhouse and its office, are still standing and still lived in today. Most of the housing around them came later. Ranches and split-levels went up through the 1950s, 60s, and 70s, on lots that run larger than Bend's average. Because the neighborhood grew up house by house over four decades rather than as a single platted subdivision, the housing stock is a real mix of eras and conditions, not a matched set from one builder.

There is no HOA here and no covenant governing what a house can look like. The Orchard District Neighborhood Association is a volunteer, city-recognized group, one of 13 neighborhood districts the City of Bend formally designates, and it operates as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that asks for voluntary donations rather than mandatory dues or assessments. Its early projects included Laurel Pocket Park, Franklin's Corner Community Garden, and a cleanup effort called Let's Pull Together.

Bend Source's reporting on neighborhood census data puts Orchard well ahead of the rest of the city on racial diversity, with roughly twice the Black population and three times the Latinx population found in other Bend neighborhoods, plus a younger, more millennial-heavy mix of residents.

Bend-La Pine Schools covers the neighborhood at both ends of grade school. Juniper Elementary, on the west side of Pilot Butte, is the district's technology magnet. Every student works through a Code.org computer-science curriculum starting in kindergarten, and the Oregon Department of Education has named the school a Model School at a Level 5, its highest rating. From there, kids move on to Pilot Butte Middle School at 1501 NE Neff Road.

The neighborhood's biggest landmark sits on its doorstep rather than inside it. Pilot Butte State Scenic Viewpoint, the 114-acre cinder cone the state accepted as a donated park in 1927, forms the entire eastern edge and rises to 4,141 feet at its summit. Three trails climb it on foot year-round, and a paved summit road opens seasonally, from May 1 through September 30, for anyone who would rather drive up to the same view of the Three Sisters, Mount Jefferson, and Mount Hood.

On the north side, Hollinshead Park keeps 16.5 acres of a former working ranch at 1235 NE Jones Road, land the Hollinshead and Ray families began selling to the park district in 1982. Bend Park and Recreation built it out through the 1990s and updated it again under a 2010 master plan. Today it holds a 90-plot community garden allocated by spring lottery and supported by OSU Extension Master Gardeners, a WaterWise demonstration garden, an unfenced off-leash dog area, and the Hollinshead-Matson Homestead Museum, a restored sharecropper's house that opens to visitors the second Saturday of the month from May through October. A few blocks south, the district's Juniper Swim and Fitness Center at 800 NE 6th Street runs a covered 50-meter pool, a separate indoor 25-meter pool, and more than 200 group fitness classes a week, with weekday doors open by 5:30 in the morning.

What that adds up to is a neighborhood for buyers who want an established, walkable part of Bend and are fine trading a builder's uniform streetscape for one that grew organically. There are no shared amenities to fund through dues, but no guarantee the house next door matches yours in age or style either. The honest downside is the west edge. Streets closest to the BNSF line and the US-97 Parkway sit nearer rail and highway noise than the ones closer to Pilot Butte, so where a property lands inside those boundaries matters as much as landing inside them at all.

amenities.name: Pilot Butte State Scenic Viewpoint
amenities.description: A 114-acre cinder cone on US-20 rising nearly 500 feet, with three hiking trails to the 4,141-foot summit and Cascade views. Donated to Oregon in 1927.
amenities.access: Trails year-round; summit road May 1 to September 30

amenities.name: Hollinshead Park
amenities.description: A 16.5-acre former ranch at 1235 NE Jones Road with a 90-plot community garden, a WaterWise demonstration garden, the 1940s Hollinshead-Matson Homestead Museum, an off-leash dog area, and a canal-side trail.

amenities.name: Juniper Swim and Fitness Center
amenities.description: A Bend Park and Recreation facility at 800 NE 6th Street with a 50-meter Olympic pool, an indoor 25-meter pool, a seasonal outdoor pool with a slide, and 200-plus weekly fitness classes.

amenities.name: Juniper Elementary
amenities.description: A Bend-La Pine Schools technology magnet on the west side of Pilot Butte, offering a Code.org computer-science curriculum K-5.

amenities.name: Pilot Butte Middle School
amenities.description: The Bend-La Pine Schools middle school serving the Orchard District, at 1501 NE Neff Road.

amenities.name: NE 6th Street Neighborhood Greenway
amenities.description: One of Bend's first neighborhood greenways, from Greenwood Avenue to Butler Market Road, with speed humps, crosswalks, and pedestrian and cyclist priority.
